extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, and sociologists studying news production
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying sociological criteria for how news is produced, packaged, and deemed newsworthy — including routines, typifications, sourcing, narrative forms, and institutional legitimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typification of occurrences
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworkers and news organizations draw on past experiences to 'typify' occurrences — classifying them into recognizable news-event types (spot news, soft news, continuing news, 'what-a-story', etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typifications objectify a news rhythm and facilitate processing; they are subject to revision and reformulation when events deviate. Example: Watergate was successively typified as a 'break-in' (spot news), an investigative conspiracy (soft news), a scandal prompting comment (spot), continuing investigations, and finally a presidential resignation ('what-a-story').

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadlines and objectified news rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: News production imposes deadlines and a uniform rhythm of processing upon occurrences, objectifying stages of reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadlines determine which stages of processing get prioritized and constrain what can be developed into a packaged news item; they function as both constraint and resource for newsmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routinized processing anchored in legitimated institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: News nets and coverage routines are based on expectations about how occurrences at legitimated institutions will unfold, enabling editors to plan reporter allocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predicting continuing stories (courts, legislatures, executives) lets managers schedule spot coverage and anticipate redispersion for reaction stories; this anchoring affirms institutional legitimacy by routinely seeking official comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness via institutions and aggregated quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Representativeness in news is thought to rest in 'legitimated institutions' (governors, senators, party leaders) or in amassed numbers of supporters rather than in individual citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices like quoting both major parties or using 'man/woman on the street' comments treat institutions or aggregated samples as embodiments of the public, not as direct representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional autonomy and negotiated practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworkers operate with relative unsupervision, allowing them to claim professionalism and to modify or ignore organizational rules through ongoing negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors, bureau chiefs, and reporters negotiate who covers what and how; behaviors such as sharing/hoarding information, reading colleagues' copy, and socializing shape tacit norms about work and sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual constitution of facts and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts, the need for facts, sources, and reporting methods are mutually self-constituting: methods for identifying facts also objectify social life and can reify phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not a claim of pure relativism but an observation that professional methods and validated sources shape what is treated as factual; selection of sources helps construct the facticity of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reification of economic activity and civil disorders
rubrics_metrics.description: News often presents economic fluctuations and civil disorders as alien, non-human, or natural forces (reification), making them appear beyond individual control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television visuals and narrative frames treat riots and economic shifts like weather phenomena; consequence: individuals are portrayed as powerless and public response is framed as sympathy rather than political organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of centralized/legitimated authorities as primary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: To present facts, newsworkers rely on centralized, official sources responsible for handling crises (governors, military officers, economic advisors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting officials both informs viewers and legitimates the authorities' actions; success or failure of officials is framed as interaction with reified forces, which reinforces institutional legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as soothing / narcotizing function
rubrics_metrics.description: News consumption can produce a narcotizing dysfunction where being informed substitutes for taking action; consumers mistake knowledge for doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lazarsfeld and Merton's formulation: secondary media contact makes individuals feel concerned and informed but not mobilized to act; prominent, remote journalists/personae reinforce the passive relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequenced Q&A frames that limit perception of innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionally validated sequences of questions and answers impose frames on events and can create a 'trained incapacity' to grasp innovations or new ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without appropriate questions, reporters may dismiss, mock, or transform innovations into soft news or nonnews; typifications and routine Q&A sequences encourage blindness to novel significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational constraints that determine news status
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical constraints — press of work, omnipresence of deadlines, and the struggle to present factual accounts — determine whether an occurrence becomes spot news, soft news, or nonnews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an event cannot be easily fit into a known narrative form within constraints, it will require more time (soft news) or be dismissed; these constraints are organizationally and professionally objectified as reasons for coverage choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: News narrative forms (web of facticity) shape what is reportable
rubrics_metrics.description: The representational forms and narrative logic of news (its 'web of facticity') bound and structure what can and will be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to university courses or scientific article formats, news narrative forms make certain topics speakable and others marginal; this structuring legitimates particular accounts and the status quo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim to professionalism and First Amendment rights as legitimating devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The profession's claims (professionalism, private property rights, First Amendment protections) legitimize both the newsworkers' role and the news itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These claims are invoked to defend journalistic practices and to assert authority, thereby reinforcing the social authority and gatekeeping functions of news organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as a social resource of knowledge and power
rubrics_metrics.description: News is a constructed source of knowledge that functions as a social resource and a means to distribute or suppress knowledge and thus exercise power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because knowledge confers power, newsmaking choices about framing and dissemination limit analytic understanding of social life and tend to legitimate existing social, political, and economic arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retypification when events deviate (appeal to precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: When occurrences do not unfold as predicted, newsworkers retype or reinterpret them, often invoking historical precedent to make them intelligible and newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: President Johnson's decision not to run was reinterpreted by invoking Calvin Coolidge's precedent; retypification can itself be presented as evidence of newsworthiness and reaffirm routines.
